title: Obligation and Service Level Tracking
answer: Obligation and service level tracking is the practice of identifying, recording, and monitoring the promises and performance targets that a contract creates. It covers payment terms, delivery dates, uptime commitments, support response times, reporting duties, renewal notice windows, and remedies for missed targets. In the contract lifecycle, it sits after drafting and signature, where the text becomes an operating checklist for legal, finance, procurement, and service teams. The work connects what a contract says to what actually happens, so that a missed obligation is visible before it becomes a dispute.

sections.body: Obligation and service level tracking is the practice of identifying, recording, and monitoring the promises and performance targets that a contract creates. It covers payment terms, delivery dates, uptime commitments, support response times, reporting duties, renewal notice windows, and remedies for missed targets. In the contract lifecycle, it sits after drafting and signature, where the text becomes an operating checklist for legal, finance, procurement, and service teams. The work connects what a contract says to what actually happens, so that a missed obligation is visible before it becomes a dispute.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems usually run on a contract repository or a contract lifecycle management platform, with connectors to email, ticketing, billing, and enterprise resource planning tools. The data layer holds clause text, extracted metadata, obligation owners, due dates, service level definitions, and measurement history. Alerts and dashboards sit on top, often delivered through a web application, a spreadsheet export, or a workflow tool. Where machine learning is used, it typically runs as a hosted service or an on premises model that reads contract language and classifies obligations.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with ingestion, where signed contracts and amendments are parsed and split into clauses. Extraction models or rules identify obligation language, service level metrics, measurement windows, and notice periods, then a reviewer confirms or corrects the output. Each obligation is assigned an owner, a due date, a source clause, and a tracking method, such as a calendar reminder, a ticket, or a live metric feed. During the contract term, the system compares actual performance against the service level, records evidence, and raises an escalation when a threshold is breached or a deadline approaches.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on confidentiality, privilege, data protection, and the provenance of extracted text. Teams need to know which contract version a tracked obligation came from, who changed it, and whether the underlying model was trained or tuned on sensitive data. Audit trails, access controls, and retention rules matter because obligation records can become evidence in a dispute or a regulatory review. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages show how quickly the surrounding rules can shift, so provenance and human review are practical controls, not paperwork.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter coupling between contract text and operational systems, so that a service level breach in a monitoring tool can trigger a contract notice or a credit automatically. Drafting tools are beginning to suggest clauses that are already mapped to trackable metrics, which reduces the gap between what is signed and what is measured. Expect more standard data models for obligations and service levels, and more scrutiny of how automated tracking handles ambiguity, change control, and disputed evidence. The field will likely remain a mix of extraction, workflow, and human judgment rather than a fully autonomous compliance engine.
